A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
WT1 is a gene for Wilms' tumor and that it may also be a gene for other tumors and for leukemia/lymphomas.

Wilms' tumor is not a single disease, but rather a complex of diseases with different etiologies, and that WT is a syndrome with many manifestations, not only genitourinary and renal, but also hematologic, and that the syndrome is genetically heterogeneous.
Wilms' tumor and leukemia/lymphomas are more common in families with Li-Fraumenin syndrome than would be expected by chance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk for leukemia/lymphomas is increased among families with WT.
the WT gene on chromosome 1lp13, which has been shown to be mutated in a number of Wilms' tumors, may also play a role in the development of leukemia and lymphomas.

WT1 is not only involved in the development of Wilms' tumors but also in other types of cancer, such as leukemias and lymphoma, which is consistent with the hypothesis that WT1 plays a role in normal development and differentiation.
